slides.title: When does breaking a problem into smaller tasks help?
slides.notes:
Separate three things: splits chosen by code, learned question lists, and learned next actions.

The model can use its prior knowledge, but we have not shown a general learned recursive strategy. Examples on the next two slides.

slides.title: Can the model learn which smaller questions to ask?
slides.notes:
We taught 256 example question lists. The model saw the original question and document titles, then proposed a list before helpers answered.

The final model could read all documents and sometimes answer without a useful plan.

slides.title: A crafting game makes the outcome easy to check.
slides.notes:
Invented lantern example. Two sticks make a frame. Frame plus glowing stone makes a lantern.

Success requires the requested net increase in target items at finish. No partial credit. Selected TextCraft-Synth panels, not the full official benchmark.

slides.title: Good examples show why the next step matters.
slides.notes:
The expert knew the solution. The learner did not always see the observation that made the next action relevant.

We reordered existing lookups and rebuilt observations, keeping all 366 taught actions. Longer inputs and easier copying may explain part of the gain.

slides.title: The repair helped after retraining and on more goals.
slides.notes:
Each row tests eight goals in two worlds twice. There are sixteen distinct goals in all.

We kept actions and update counts fixed, not total compute. More original training and discovery-based teaching are important controls.

slides.title: Let code write the known ingredient list.
slides.notes:
323/768 = 42.1%; 381/768 = 49.6%. Forty-eight goals across worlds and seeds, not 768 independent tasks. Same weights within pairs.

Code writes observed ingredients only. It neither creates materials nor selects the plan.

slides.title: We also tested letting code do the arithmetic.
slides.notes:
Neither model was retrained. Numeric matches rose from 51 to 108/508 for 4B, and 52 to 102 for 8B. Each method made one call per question.

Rounding, reference errors and previously seen examples limit the claim. This is not a new arithmetic method.

slides.title: What did we learn from reward training?
slides.notes:
The extra success after two RL updates was lost after the third. Extra SFT also scored 4/16, but one SFT step is not matched to three RL steps.

Earlier MuSiQue answering improved with both RL and extra SFT. We need fresh problems and fair controls.

slides.title: The broader tests changed how we interpret progress.
slides.notes:
The candidate split was programmed. It helped on twelve cases, but used more text.

New news articles weakened the RL gain. In MRCR, retrieval stayed the same while exact reproduction improved. Ask which ability actually changed.

slides.title: Can the teaching repair survive stronger tests?
slides.notes:
Next: test new problems, stronger teaching alternatives, more training and another model. These tests are proposed, not newly launched.

Others already study demonstration repair. We need to show what this particular repair adds and where it fails.
